title: 'Brotherhood' Trailer: A Musical About Immigration, Empathy, and the Power of Neighborly Love
summary:
If you've been following IndieWire's "A Producer's Path" columns, you know Daren Smith has been using his upcoming film "Brotherhood: A Cinematic Musical" as a case study for independent filmmaking in 2026. Now, the film is almost ready to unveil to the world.

Written and directed by Ross Boothe, who also composed 13 original songs, "Brotherhood" tells the story of two next-door neighbors whose lives become deeply intertwined. Jon (Casey Elliott, a founding member of the tenor group GENTRI) is a lifelong American citizen, while Fabián (Broadway star Mauricio Martínez) is a Mexican immigrant who has spent more than a decade waiting for a resolution to his U.S. asylum application. As the men and their families navigate uncertainty and turbulence, they are challenged to see one another beyond labels and to rediscover what it truly means to be neighbors, Americans, and human beings.

For Martínez, the role is deeply personal. "As an immigrant, this story hits very close to home right now," he said in a statement. "It's about people, about heart, and about empathy—and music is such a powerful way to communicate those things. That's what moved me most about 'Brotherhood.'"

Before the film's release, Boothe, Martínez, and Elliott will embark on the Love Your Neighbor tour, featuring live performances, select scenes from the film, and roundtable discussions led by cultural lead Liliana Bolaños with local leaders, authors, and special guests. The tour kicks off August 29 in Salt Lake City and ends October 1 in New York. "Brotherhood: A Cinematic Musical" opens in select theaters on Friday, October 9.

So if you're looking for a film that combines catchy songs with a timely story about connection, mark your calendar. This one might just make you want to knock on your neighbor's door.
why_it_matters: The film puts a human face on immigration and asylum at a time when debates about borders and belonging are intensifying across the U.S.; art like this can shape how communities treat newcomers and influence local conversations about policy.

perspectives.description: Supporters see the film and tour as a humanizing look at immigrants awaiting asylum, using music and storytelling to build empathy across political and cultural divides.

Skeptics may argue that a musical can oversimplify immigration policy or reduce complex legal struggles to emotional appeal. Some may also question whether a feel-good story actually changes laws or material outcomes for asylum seekers.

The film represents a broader trend of independent filmmakers using personal stories and community events to reach audiences outside traditional blockbuster marketing. It shows how faith, art, and local leadership can become part of a film's distribution strategy.

If the Love Your Neighbor tour sparks sustained local conversations, it could influence how community and faith groups engage with immigration issues after the film leaves theaters. The next test is whether empathy translates into policy change or concrete support.
